strengths: The core idea of decomposing moiré images into high-frequency (texture) and low-frequency (color) components, and applying tailored crop/resize training strategies to each, is well-motivated by clear empirical observations (Fig. 2, Table 3) showing the frequency-dependent robustness properties.

The learnable Frequency Composition Transform (FCT) is a reasonable improvement over fixed inverse composition, and the ablations (Table 4) show consistent, if modest, gains from this component across two backbones (ESDNet and Freqformer).
The proposed frequency decomposition is shown empirically to substantially outperform a Haar-wavelet baseline, supporting the paper's claim that better frequency separation matters for this task.

The method achieves competitive or state-of-the-art PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on FHDMi and UHDM with a notably smaller parameter count (6.065M) than most competitors, and low FLOPs suitable for 4K images, which is a practically relevant contribution for deployment.

The ablation studies are reasonably thorough, isolating the effects of resize vs. crop training, learnable vs. fixed FCT, hierarchical fusion, RDDB, and per-branch performance, which supports the internal consistency of the design choices.
Related work coverage is broad and situates the method relative to prior wavelet-based, CNN-based, video, and raw-domain demoiréing works.
weaknesses: The gains on UHDM are marginal and mixed: Freqformer is second in PSNR (22.22 vs 22.42 for ESDNet-L) despite having fewer parameters, and the SSIM/LPIPS improvements over ESDNet-L are very small, raising questions about the practical significance of the improvement versus run-to-run variance; no variance/multiple-run statistics are reported.
The two-stage training procedure adds complexity and hyperparameters (crop size, resize size, lambda1, lambda2, epochs per stage) that are not clearly justified via a sensitivity analysis.

The choice of decomposition kernel/levels is inspired by prior work but the paper does not clearly ablate the number of decomposition levels L or alternative kernel designs beyond the single Haar comparison.

The claim that the low-frequency branch can be aggressively downsampled and still reconstructed with high PSNR is measured on the decomposition/recomposition process itself rather than after the network corrects color distortions, so the link to end-task performance is somewhat indirect.

Comparisons against very recent, large diffusion/all-in-one restoration baselines are informative but these models are not designed for demoiréing; more demoiréing-specific recent SOTA methods discussed in related work (e.g., P-BiC, DMSFN, MoiréDet) are not included in the quantitative tables.
Some notational/presentation issues remain, and the dense pipeline description (Fig. 3/4) could benefit from clearer textual walkthrough for reproducibility.
Inference-time latency/runtime is only partially reported (FLOPs and a single speed column in one ablation table), leaving efficiency claims for edge deployment only partially substantiated.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: it explicitly analyzes (via 2D/3D RGB curve visualization in Fig. 2) that moiré texture corruption concentrates in high-frequency components while color distortion concentrates in low-frequency components, which directly justifies the dual-branch design.

The proposed crop-based (high-frequency) vs. resize-based (low-frequency) training strategy is a sensible, empirically supported design choice (Table 3 shows resize clearly outperforms crop/crop-tile for the low branch, and this holds for both Freqformer and a retrained ESDNet-L baseline).

Reasonably extensive ablations are provided: learnable vs. fixed FCT, end-to-end vs. two-branch training, per-branch performance vs. ESDNet, hierarchical fusion and RDDB contributions, and a direct comparison against Haar-wavelet-based decomposition.

The method achieves a favorable performance/efficiency trade-off, reaching SOTA or near-SOTA PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on FHDMi and UHDM with substantially fewer parameters (6.065M) and lower FLOPs than several baselines (MopNet, MBCNN, AdaIR, MoCE-IR, OSEDiff), which is relevant for high-resolution/edge deployment.
Comparisons include not only demoiréing-specific baselines but also recent general image-restoration models (AdaIR, MoCE-IR, OSEDiff), broadening the scope of the empirical evaluation.
weaknesses: On the harder UHDM benchmark, Freqformer is only second-best in PSNR (22.22 vs. ESDNet-L's 22.42), and margins over ESDNet-L in SSIM/LPIPS are marginal (e.g., 0.8018 vs 0.7985 SSIM, 0.2434 vs 0.2454 LPIPS); the 'state-of-the-art' framing is somewhat overstated given these small, single-run differences with no reported variance across seeds/runs.

The forward frequency decomposition (Eq. 1-2, a fixed Gaussian-like recursive kernel akin to a Laplacian-pyramid decomposition) is itself non-learnable, yet the paper's stated motivation criticizes wavelet-based methods for using 'predefined, non-trainable' transforms; only the inverse composition (FCT) is learnable, so the novelty claim over wavelet approaches is partially overstated and the core decomposition mechanism itself is not particularly novel (related to standard multiscale/Laplacian decomposition ideas already used elsewhere, e.g., [37]).

The Haar-transform ablation used to justify the proposed decomposition produces an extreme failure (PSNR 13.32 vs. ~25 for the proposed method), which is suspicious and suggests either an unfair/under-tuned comparison or an implementation issue; a more controlled, apples-to-apples comparison (same backbone, tuned hyperparameters for both decomposition types) would strengthen this key claim.

The two-stage training pipeline (separate branch pretraining, then joint fine-tuning with FCT) introduces additional hyperparameters (crop/resize sizes per dataset, λ1, λ2, epoch schedule) that are manually tuned per dataset, raising reproducibility and generalization concerns to new datasets/scenes not covered by FHDMi/UHDM.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple-run variance is reported anywhere, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (often <0.5 dB PSNR or <0.005 SSIM) are meaningful versus noise.

The paper lacks any discussion of failure cases, limitations, or scenarios where the frequency decomposition might break down (e.g., moiré patterns whose spectral content overlaps substantially with real high-frequency image content, or scenes with strong global illumination gradients affecting the low-frequency assumption).

Minor writing/clarity issues: some notation in Eq. 4-5 is loosely defined (e.g., PostFusion, dimensional consistency), a typo ('reals' should be 'reveals') in Sec. 3.2, and dense architectural description in Sec. 3.2/Fig. 4 that could benefit from clearer notation and a summary table of module design choices.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated limitation of prior frequency-decomposition demoiréing methods (naive wavelet concatenation, multi-stage error accumulation) with a clearly articulated alternative: an efficient, learnable frequency decomposition that separates moiré artifacts into high-frequency texture and low-frequency color distortion components, backed by an intuitive and convincing visualization (Fig. 2/RGB curve analysis) that motivates the design choice.

The dual-branch design is well justified with an ablation showing that Haar-transform-based decomposition catastrophically fails (PSNR 13.32) compared to the proposed decomposition, supporting the core technical claim that the choice of frequency transform matters substantially for this task.

The crop-for-high-frequency / resize-for-low-frequency training strategy is empirically supported (Table 3) with consistent improvements shown on both Freqformer and an independently retrained ESDNet-L, strengthening generality of the finding beyond just the proposed architecture.

Strong quantitative results on FHDMi with a clear improvement margin over prior SOTA, and competitive/near-best results on the more challenging UHDM dataset with substantially fewer parameters (6.065M) than most competitors (e.g., MopNet 58.565M, MBCNN 14.192M, ESDNet-L 10.623M), plus favorable comparisons against much larger general restoration models (AdaIR, MoCE-IR, OSEDiff with ~950M parameters).

Extensive and fairly thorough ablation studies covering the FCT module, hierarchical fusion, RDDB, per-branch performance, and the resize-vs-crop strategy, which collectively give good insight into which components drive the gains.
Reasonable efficiency profiling (TFLOPs, params) supporting the practical deployment claims for high-resolution/edge scenarios.
weaknesses: On the UHDM dataset, the PSNR improvement over ESDNet-L is marginal/inverted (22.22 vs 22.42, Freqformer is actually second-best), which slightly undercuts the 'state-of-the-art' framing in the abstract/intro for the harder benchmark; the paper should be more precise about where gains are strongest versus marginal.

The proposed frequency decomposition operator (Eq. 1-2), while empirically effective, is not theoretically analyzed—there's no formal characterization of why this particular convolution kernel/recursive scheme better separates moiré-induced high/low frequency content than Haar wavelets beyond the empirical comparison; a more principled or spectral analysis would strengthen the contribution's soundness.

The two-stage training procedure (separate branch pretraining followed by joint fine-tuning with FCT) adds complexity and additional hyperparameters (crop/resize sizes, λ1, λ2, number of levels L is not explicitly stated) that are not fully ablated—e.g., sensitivity to the number of decomposition levels L or to λ1/λ2 is not studied.

Comparison with recent frequency-based baselines (e.g., WDNet, MBWDN, AWUDN) is somewhat limited in Table 1 (WDNet only, N/A for FHDMi), and MBWDN/AWUDN mentioned in related work are not directly compared quantitatively, which weakens the direct empirical case against the closest competing paradigm.

Reproducibility could be improved: several implementation details (e.g., exact value of decomposition level L, exact architecture dimensions/hidden sizes, how λ1/λ2 were tuned) are not fully specified in the main text, and code availability is only promised, not verifiable at review time.

The claim that low-frequency resizing 'preserves full color information compactly' and can be aggressively downsampled is empirically demonstrated only via reconstruction PSNR sanity checks (~50dB) rather than a more rigorous information-theoretic or task-specific justification; edge cases (e.g., images with large low-frequency color gradients or unusual lighting) are not stress-tested.

strengths: Well-motivated frequency decomposition scheme using a Gaussian-like smoothing kernel with recursive residual structure that avoids the spatial discontinuity, resolution loss, and channel-redundancy problems of Haar wavelets and block DCT, with clear conceptual justification (Fig. 2, Fig. 3) and empirical validation (Table 3).

The asymmetric crop/resize training strategy is a sensible design that exploits the different spatial statistics of high- vs low-frequency components (locality vs scale-robustness), and is empirically validated via reconstruction PSNR experiments (Sec 3.2) and ablations (Table 4) showing large gains from resizing on the low branch.

Extensive experiments across four standard demoiréing benchmarks (TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, UHDM) against a wide range of baselines (CNN-based, transformer-based, diffusion-based, RAW-domain, video demoireing) show consistently strong or state-of-the-art performance with a notably compact model (6.065M parameters) and competitive FLOPs, suggesting a good efficiency-performance trade-off.

Thorough ablation studies decompose contributions of each proposed component (frequency decomposition choice, resize training, learnable FCT, SA-CA module design choices including RDDB vs deeper transformer, SCP vs full conv, and DAT baseline), which supports the internal validity of the design choices and aids reproducibility of the architecture rationale.

Learnable FCT module is a reasonable improvement over naive addition-based composition, since it allows fusing branch features in a way that can mitigate coincident reconstruction errors, and its benefit is empirically shown (Table 5).
weaknesses: The core frequency decomposition kernel is stated as 'inspired by Wang et al. [33]', but the paper does not clearly delineate what aspect is genuinely novel versus adapted; the technical distinction from a simple binomial/Gaussian blur pyramid (which is a well-known classical technique) should be more rigorously justified beyond empirical superiority over Haar/DCT.

The two-stage training procedure (independent branch training followed by joint fine-tuning) adds complexity and additional hyperparameters (e.g., number of epochs per stage, respective loss weighting) that are not fully detailed, raising reproducibility concerns; code availability is promised but not yet provided.

On the most challenging UHDM (real-world 4K) dataset, Freqformer is second in PSNR (Table 1), and in Table 2 it is inferior to OSEDiff in LPIPS, suggesting the method's advantages may be less pronounced on more realistic/harder distributions, which slightly tempers the generality of the state-of-the-art claim.

Model efficiency claims are mixed: while Freqformer has fewer parameters and comparable/lower FLOPs than several baselines, its actual inference speed (0.58 s/image at 4K) is over 2x slower than ESDNet-L, which the authors attribute to unoptimized attention operations; this practical latency drawback is relevant for the paper's claims about suitability for edge deployment.

The visual/quantitative gains, though consistent, are sometimes marginal against strong recent baselines (e.g., ESDNet-L in Table 1), and statistical significance or variance across runs is not reported, making it harder to assess robustness of the reported improvements.

The paper would benefit from more directly quantifying color-distortion correction and texture-restoration performance separately (beyond the illustrative PSNR-based branch reconstruction experiment in Sec 3.2) to substantiate the central claim that high/low frequency components map cleanly onto texture/color corruption, since this assumption underlies the entire architectural design.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-motivated empirical analysis (Fig. 2, Sec. 3.1/3.2) of why high- and low-frequency components of moiré images behave differently (strong locality vs. scale-robustness), and uses this analysis to justify the dual-branch, asymmetric crop/resize training scheme — a practical and reasonably novel design insight for this task.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four demoiréing benchmarks (TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, UHDM) and comparison against a wide range of baselines, including CNN-based demoiréing methods, wavelet/DCT frequency-based methods, RAW-domain and video demoiréing models, and even general-purpose/diffusion-based restoration models (AdaIR, MoCE-IR, OSEDiff).

Reasonable model efficiency: Freqformer achieves competitive or state-of-the-art PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS with a notably smaller parameter count (6.065M) than several competitors (MopNet 58.6M, MBCNN 14.2M), and comparable FLOPs to ESDNet variants.

Extensive and informative ablation studies (Tables 3–6) isolating the contributions of the frequency decomposition choice (vs. Haar DWT and block DCT), the resize-based low-frequency training strategy, the learnable FCT fusion module, and architectural components (RDDB, SCP, hierarchical fusion, SA-CA vs. DAT), which support the design choices with quantitative evidence.
The paper candidly reports a limitation (slower wall-clock inference than ESDNet-L despite lower FLOPs) rather than hiding it, which strengthens credibility.
weaknesses: The core frequency decomposition (Eq. 1–3) is a fixed, non-learnable Gaussian/Laplacian-pyramid-style low-pass filter directly adapted from prior work (Wang et al. [33]); despite being framed as a key contribution, the decomposition itself is not learnable (only the fusion/FCT stage is), and conceptually resembles a classical Laplacian pyramid, so the novelty of the "frequency decomposition" contribution is more incremental than the paper's framing suggests.

The overall architecture is an assembly of existing components (RDDB blocks, channel attention, gated FFN, Gaussian pyramid decomposition, PixelShuffle fusion) with the main new elements being the specific combination, the asymmetric crop/resize training schedule, and the lightweight FCT fusion — the degree of genuine algorithmic innovation is modest.

Ablation studies are conducted only on FHDMi; it is unclear whether the same design choices (decomposition kernel, resize strategy, FCT, SA-CA vs. DAT) generalize to the other three benchmarks, limiting confidence in the robustness of the reported design decisions.

On the more challenging UHDM dataset, Freqformer is only second-best in PSNR (behind ESDNet-L) and is outperformed by OSEDiff in LPIPS on both FHDMi and UHDM, indicating the proposed method does not uniformly dominate across all metrics/datasets despite the state-of-the-art framing.

The two-stage training procedure (independent branch pretraining followed by joint fine-tuning with FCT) adds practical complexity and additional hyperparameters/training cost that are not deeply analyzed (e.g., sensitivity to stage-two learning rate, number of epochs per stage, or training-time overhead relative to single-stage baselines).

No reported variance/multiple-seed results, and some quantitative tables suffer from OCR/formatting artifacts in the provided PDF that make a few entries hard to parse precisely, slightly hindering full verification of the magnitude of improvements.
Code availability is only promised ("will be made publicly available"), so reproducibility cannot currently be verified.

strengths: Well-motivated frequency decomposition strategy that addresses concrete limitations of DWT/DCT (spatial discontinuity, shift-variance, block artifacts, channel redundancy), supported by clear visual/statistical analysis (Fig. 2) showing high-frequency components carry texture/structure differences while low-frequency components carry color-shift information.

Sensible dual-branch, asymmetric training design (crop for high-frequency, resize for low-frequency) motivated by empirically measured reconstruction PSNR under resizing (~25dB vs ~50dB), which is a nice piece of supporting evidence for an otherwise heuristic design choice.

Extensive and fairly convincing ablation studies (Tables 3–6) that isolate the contributions of the proposed frequency transform vs. Haar/DCT, the resize-based low-branch training vs. crop/tile, the learnable FCT vs. fixed composition and single-branch baselines, and individual architectural components (RDDB vs. deeper transformer, SCP vs. full conv, SA-CA vs. DAT block).

Broad experimental comparison across four demoiréing benchmarks (TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, UHDM) plus comparisons against general image-restoration and diffusion-based restoration methods (AdaIR, MoCE-IR, OSEDiff) and RAW/video demoireing baselines (RRID, STD-Net, DTNet), showing competitive or SOTA performance with a notably smaller model (6.065M parameters) and reasonable FLOPs.

Reasonably detailed implementation/reproducibility information (crop sizes, optimizer, schedule, epochs, batch size, per-branch depth settings) and clear formalization of the decomposition and FCT modules with equations.
weaknesses: Ablation studies are conducted only on the FHDMi dataset; it is not verified whether the same design choices (frequency decomposition, resize strategy, FCT, SA-CA) generalize equally well across the other three benchmarks, which somewhat limits the strength of the ablation conclusions.

On the more challenging UHDM dataset, Freqformer is second in PSNR (behind ESDNet-L), and inference speed is slower than ESDNet-L despite lower FLOPs; this efficiency trade-off is acknowledged but not analyzed or mitigated, leaving the practical deployment claim ("suitable for edge devices") partly unsubstantiated.

The proposed convolutional decomposition kernel is explicitly adapted from a prior work (Wang et al. [33]) originally used for a different purpose (diffusion-based super-resolution); while attribution is given, the paper could more clearly delineate what is genuinely novel in the decomposition design versus what is borrowed.
Code is only promised ("will be made publicly available") rather than provided, so full reproducibility cannot currently be verified.

The paper lacks an explicit discussion of failure cases/limitations of the proposed method (e.g., scenarios where the high/low frequency split may not cleanly separate moiré from texture) and does not discuss broader societal impact, which would strengthen the completeness of the submission though their absence is not disqualifying.

Minor clarity issues: some notation (e.g., feature naming F̂ vs F, and the loss terms in Eq. 8–10) could be explained more explicitly for readers unfamiliar with the deep supervision scheme from [53]; the two-stage training procedure and the crop-to-full-size feature interpolation step (for FCT fusion) could benefit from a clearer algorithmic description.
